name: Ater
title: Ancestor of returning families and the gatekeeper lineage
summary: Ater is a name that appears several times in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, and likely refers to at least two or three different individuals. Ater's descendants 'of Hezekiah' formed a group of 98 people who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. In addition, Ater is mentioned among the priestly families of gatekeepers who served at the temple after the return. A man named Ater was also among the leaders who sealed the covenant to follow God's law in Nehemiah's time. The name testifies to the many families that contributed to the rebuilding of the Jewish community after the exile.

footnotes.text: The name Ater (Hebrew: אָטֵר, 'Ater) likely means 'closed' or 'bound', possibly referring to a physical trait such as a crippled hand. Some scholars link it to a root meaning 'to shut again'.

In Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, Ater appears in two different contexts: first as the ancestor of a family group of 98 people 'of Hezekiah' (possibly a branch of Hezekiah's royal line), and then as a lineage of gatekeepers. This suggests that at least two different individuals bore this name.

The Gatekeepers (Hebrew: שׁוֹעֲרִים, sho'arim) had an important role in temple service. They guarded the temple gates, controlled access, and ensured that ritual purity was maintained. This service traced its roots back to David's organization of temple worship.

The sealing of the covenant in Nehemiah 10 was a solemn renewal of the agreement in which the people's leaders committed themselves to keep God's law. Ater was among the leaders who placed their seal on this document, testifying to his position and influence in the restored community.
